neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person and place; knows month and year but states the date is three days off. MMSE 21/30, losing points on recall (0/3 at 5 minutes, no improvement with cues), orientation (2 points lost), serial sevens (3 errors), and pentagons (unable to draw intersecting pentagons accurately). Clock drawing shows numbers clustered on the right side with hour hand placed at the correct number but minute hand pointing to the number 10 rather than the 2 o'clock position. Naming intact for common objects, difficulty naming the band on a watch ('that thing that holds it on'). Repetition intact. Follows two-step commands but fails three-step commands. neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, reactive to light. Extraocular movements full without nystagmus. Visual fields full to confrontation. Face symmetric at rest and with activation. Hearing reduced bilaterally (known hearing loss, wearing aids). Palate elevates symmetrically. Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius strength 5/5 bilaterally. Tongue midline, no fasciculations or atrophy.
neurological_exam.motor: Bulk and tone normal throughout. No cogwheel rigidity. Strength 5/5 in all extremities. No pronator drift. No tremor, asterixis, or involuntary movements.
neurological_exam.sensory: Intact to light touch, pinprick, vibration, and proprioception in upper extremities. Mildly reduced vibration sense at bilateral great toes (consistent with age and diabetes). Proprioception intact distally.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ and symmetric at biceps, triceps, brachioradialis bilaterally. Patellar reflexes 2+ bilaterally. Achilles reflexes 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffman sign.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin normal bilaterally. No dysmetria or intention tremor. Rapid alternating movements intact.
neurological_exam.gait: Steady gait with normal base and stride. Mild hesitation on tandem gait but completes without falling. Romberg negative. No festination, no retropulsion.
neurological_exam.additional: No paratonic rigidity. No grasp reflexes. No snout or palmomental reflexes. No myoclonus. Frontal release signs absent.

patient.chief_complaint: Progressive memory loss and trouble managing finances over the past two years
patient.history_present_illness: Mr. Harold Jenkins is a 74-year-old right-handed retired postal service supervisor who presents to the neurology memory clinic accompanied by his wife, Gloria, and adult daughter, Denise, for evaluation of progressive memory difficulties that have worsened steadily over the past two years. His wife first noticed problems approximately two years ago when Mr. Jenkins began forgetting to pay several household bills, something he had managed independently and reliably for decades. Over the subsequent months, his daughter discovered multiple unopened bills in a drawer and noticed late payment notices accumulating. His wife gradually took over the finances approximately one year ago. He frequently repeats stories and questions within the same conversation, often unaware that he has already told them. His wife reports that he left the back door unlocked several times overnight, which is very uncharacteristic, and on one occasion left the car running in the driveway for over an hour after returning from the barbershop. He has become less engaged in his weekly card game with friends from the postal service, stating that he cannot keep track of the cards as well as he used to. His golf partners have mentioned that he occasionally forgets whose turn it is and has difficulty keeping score accurately. He struggled to program the new television remote control after they recently upgraded their cable service, whereas previously he was comfortable with technology. His wife notes that he occasionally puts items in unusual places, such as placing his wallet in the refrigerator and his reading glasses in the pantry. He continues to dress himself appropriately, manages his own grooming, and recognizes all family members without difficulty. He still drives for short familiar errands but his wife has started accompanying him due to one incident where he took a wrong turn coming home from church, a route he has driven for over thirty years. He has become somewhat more withdrawn socially and occasionally appears frustrated when he cannot find the right word during conversation. He denies any hallucinations, and his family has not observed any personality or behavioral changes apart from mild irritability when he is aware of his mistakes. There have been no episodes of confusion with fluctuating alertness, no tremor, no falls, and no changes in his walking. Sleep is reportedly normal, and his wife has not observed any acting out of dreams or unusual nocturnal behaviors.

output.impression: Neuropsychological evaluation demonstrates a predominantly amnestic profile with multi-domain involvement. Episodic memory is severely impaired: RAVLT delayed recall at the 1st percentile and immediate recall at the 3rd percentile, consistent with a storage-type encoding deficit with no benefit from cuing. Semantic fluency (Category Fluency — Animals, 8th percentile) and confrontation naming (Boston Naming Test, 15th percentile) are significantly below expected norms. Both letter fluency (FAS, 22nd percentile) and executive set-shifting (Trail Making B, 15th percentile) are mildly impaired. Visuoconstructive ability (Rey Complex Figure Copy, 20th percentile) is reduced. Processing speed (Trail Making A, 25th percentile) is at the lower limit of normal. Screening scores: MMSE 21/30, MoCA 17/30. Mood screening is borderline (GDS 5/15); cognitive deficits are disproportionate to any mood contribution. Profile is consistent with amnestic mild cognitive impairment, multi-domain type

alzheimer_management.query: Alzheimer disease late-onset management cholinesterase inhibitors

results.title: Donepezil, memantine, or both for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease
results.authors: Howard R, McShane R, Lindesay J, et al.
results.summary: Combination of donepezil and memantine provided benefits over donepezil alone for moderate to severe Alzheimer disease.

alzheimer_management.summary: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) have demonstrated modest cognitive and functional benefits in randomized controlled trials of Alzheimer's disease. Memantine has demonstrated additional benefit when added to cholinesterase inhibitor therapy in moderate-to-severe disease populations. Electrolyte and comorbidity monitoring is part of ongoing medical management. Clinical correlation recommended.

differential.key_features: DLB must be actively excluded by absence of visual hallucinations, parkinsonism, cognitive fluctuations, and REM sleep behavior disorder; biomarkers and (when needed) DaTscan can distinguish if features emerge
FTD typically presents with prominent personality change, disinhibition, or progressive aphasia rather than amnesia; positive amyloid biomarkers further argue against FTLD pathology
No significant cerebrovascular burden on MRI and the gradual amnestic course is not stepwise — pure VCI is unlikely
Insidious course over months to years with disproportionate delayed-recall impairment and limited benefit from cueing is not typical of pseudodementia

differential.diagnosis: Reversible metabolic, endocrine, or sleep-related cognitive impairment
differential.key_features: Screening labs exclude hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis, and HIV; the progressive amnestic profile would not normalize with treatment of any of these alone

optimal_actions.action: Obtain detailed clinical history from patient and informant, including timeline, cognitive domains affected, functional decline, mood, sleep, and medication review
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Gradually progressive cognitive change with informant-confirmed functional impairment in IADLs

optimal_actions.action: Perform bedside cognitive assessment (MMSE and/or MoCA) and detailed neurological examination
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Objective cognitive impairment on MoCA more sensitive than MMSE; non-focal neurological exam (or variant-specific findings — visuospatial in PCA, language in lvPPA, behavioral in frontal AD)

optimal_actions.action: Order reversible-cause labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, vitamin B12, folate; consider RPR/HIV per risk)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis) excluded; identify and address co-morbid metabolic factors

optimal_actions.action: Obtain brain MRI with dementia (volumetric) protocol to assess medial-temporal atrophy and exclude vascular disease, hippocampal sclerosis, NPH, and mass lesions
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral medial-temporal / hippocampal atrophy (Scheltens MTA grade 2-3) with temporoparietal cortical volume loss

optimal_actions.action: Order comprehensive neuropsychological testing to characterize the cognitive profile and establish a baseline for tracking
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Amnestic profile with disproportionate impairment of delayed recall and limited benefit from cueing, plus involvement of at least one other cognitive domain

optimal_actions.action: Order CSF biomarkers (Aβ42, Aβ42/40 ratio, p-tau, total tau) for ATN classification
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Reduced Aβ42 (or reduced Aβ42/40 ratio) with elevated p-tau supporting A+T+ profile consistent with Alzheimer pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order amyloid PET when CSF biomarkers are unavailable or when diagnostic uncertainty persists after clinical assessment and MRI
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Positive cortical amyloid retention (SUVr above positivity threshold) confirming amyloid pathology

optimal_actions.action: Order FDG-PET to assess regional metabolism and distinguish AD from frontotemporal dementia or other neurodegenerative patterns
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Bilateral temporoparietal and posterior cingulate hypometabolism characteristic of Alzheimer pattern

optimal_actions.action: Check drug interactions before initiating cholinesterase inhibitor (donepezil, rivastigmine, or galantamine)
optimal_actions.expected_finding: No clinically significant interactions; counsel on GI side effects and bradycardia risk

optimal_actions.action: Disclose the diagnosis to patient and family, discuss prognosis, advance directives, and driving / safety assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Patient and caregiver engaged in care planning; safety concerns (driving, finances, medication management) addressed

useless_tools.rationale: ECG is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardiac symptom or syncope to justify it in this case
Echocardiography is unrelated to the dementia workup; no cardioembolic indication in this presentation
Cardiac monitoring is not indicated; no arrhythmia, syncope, or palpitations described
Head CT adds little when MRI is available; MRI is the preferred structural modality for dementia workup

sequence_constraints.reason: Obtain structural imaging before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect / herniation risk, particularly in older patients

critical_actions: Obtain collateral history from an informant who knows the patient well
Exclude reversible causes of cognitive decline with screening labs (CBC, CMP, TSH, B12, folate; HIV/RPR per risk)
Obtain structural brain MRI with dementia/volumetric protocol
Quantify cognitive impairment with a standardized cognitive battery (MoCA at minimum; formal neuropsychological testing when feasible)
Assess safety: driving, medication management, finances, and need for caregiver support
Disclose the diagnosis and discuss prognosis, advance directives, and treatment options with the patient and family
Pursue biomarker confirmation (CSF AT(N) markers or amyloid PET) when MRI is equivocal or when an atypical AD variant is suspected
contraindicated_actions: Do not prescribe anticholinergic medications (e.g., diphenhydramine, oxybutynin, tricyclics) which worsen cognition in patients with AD
Do not prescribe benzodiazepines as first-line management of anxiety or insomnia given fall and cognitive risk
Do not start antipsychotics without a clear behavioral indication given the FDA boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia
Do not attribute symptoms entirely to normal aging, depression, or sleep apnea without completing the dementia workup
Do not start memantine monotherapy at the mild stage (memantine is approved for moderate-to-severe AD)
key_reasoning_points: Definite hippocampal and temporoparietal atrophy on MRI with a multi-domain amnestic cognitive profile is sufficient to make a clinical diagnosis of probable AD by NIA-AA 2011 criteria
The hallmark cognitive feature of AD is impaired delayed recall with rapid forgetting and limited benefit from cueing, reflecting a storage-type (hippocampal) memory deficit
APOE genotyping is a risk modifier and is not used to make the diagnosis; an E3/E4 or E4/E4 result is supportive but neither sufficient nor required for diagnosis
Low-normal B12 should prompt methylmalonic acid testing before being dismissed as a non-contributor
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line symptomatic therapy in mild-to-moderate AD; memantine is reserved for moderate-to-severe disease

key_educational_points: Early Alzheimer disease classically presents with progressive episodic memory loss as the predominant symptom
Concurrent cerebrovascular disease is common in elderly patients and does not exclude AD as the primary diagnosis
APOE e4 homozygosity (E4/E4) confers the highest genetic risk for late-onset AD
CSF biomarkers (A+T+N+ profile) can confirm neurodegenerative pathology in vivo, especially useful when concurrent vascular disease complicates the clinical picture
Cholinesterase inhibitors are first-line pharmacotherapy; vascular risk factor optimization is also important in mixed presentations
Functional assessment (finances, driving, cooking) is essential for staging and safety planning
